---
title: "Randomizing samples over plates"
subtitle: "Protect the biological comparison before the assay begins"
description: "Good and bad examples of allocating SomaScan samples across plates and well positions."
bibliography: references.bib
toc: true
---

SomaScan uses internal controls, calibration, quality-control samples, and
several normalization steps to reduce known sources of assay variation
[@somalogic2021standardization; @candia2022plasma7k]. Those procedures are
important, but they do not make experimental design irrelevant. Residual or
unanticipated technical variation can remain, and no downstream adjustment can
separate two effects that are perfectly confounded.

If all cases are placed on one plate and all controls on another, for example,
every case-control difference is also a plate difference. The data cannot tell
which explanation is responsible. Balanced block randomization is intended to
prevent this problem [@burger2021block].

::: {.callout-important}
## The design goal

Each plate should resemble a small version of the full study. Within the wells
available for study samples, spread the groups across rows, columns, edges, and
the likely processing order. Preserve any assay-control positions specified by
the performing laboratory.
:::

## Bad design: group and plate are confounded

In this simplified example, Plate 1 contains only Group A and Plate 2 contains
only Group B. A plate shift—regardless of its cause—will look exactly like a
group effect.

```{=html}
<figure class="allocation-figure" aria-labelledby="bad-plate-caption">
<div class="plate-pair">
  <div class="plate-panel">
    <div class="plate-title">Plate 1</div>
    <div class="plate-grid bad-grid" aria-label="Plate 1 contains sixteen Group A samples">
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="plate-panel">
    <div class="plate-title">Plate 2</div>
    <div class="plate-grid bad-grid" aria-label="Plate 2 contains sixteen Group B samples">
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="plate-legend"><span><i class="swatch group-a"></i> Group A</span><span><i class="swatch group-b"></i> Group B</span></div>
<figcaption id="bad-plate-caption"><strong>Bad:</strong> study group is perfectly confounded with plate. Plate adjustment cannot recover an independently estimable group effect.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

## Bad design: plate is balanced, position is not

Putting both groups on every plate is necessary, but not always sufficient.
Here, Group A always occupies the first two rows and Group B the last two rows.
Any row, edge, timing, or pipetting-order effect can still align with the
biological comparison.

```{=html}
<figure class="allocation-figure" aria-labelledby="bad-position-caption">
<div class="plate-pair">
  <div class="plate-panel">
    <div class="plate-title">Plate 1</div>
    <div class="plate-grid bad-grid" aria-label="Plate 1 has Group A in the first two rows and Group B in the final two rows">
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="plate-panel">
    <div class="plate-title">Plate 2</div>
    <div class="plate-grid bad-grid" aria-label="Plate 2 repeats Group A in the first two rows and Group B in the final two rows">
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="plate-legend"><span><i class="swatch group-a"></i> Group A</span><span><i class="swatch group-b"></i> Group B</span></div>
<figcaption id="bad-position-caption"><strong>Bad:</strong> each plate is numerically balanced, but group remains confounded with row and processing order.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

## Better design: blocked, balanced, and randomized

In the better example, both groups appear in equal numbers on each plate and
their positions change across plates. The exact map should be generated with a
recorded random seed and constrained only enough to achieve balance on the
important design variables. This distributes—not necessarily eliminates—any
remaining technical variation.

```{=html}
<figure class="allocation-figure good-allocation" aria-labelledby="good-caption">
<div class="plate-pair">
  <div class="plate-panel">
    <div class="plate-title">Plate 1</div>
    <div class="plate-grid" aria-label="Plate 1 contains a balanced mixture of Group A and Group B samples">
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="plate-panel">
    <div class="plate-title">Plate 2</div>
    <div class="plate-grid" aria-label="Plate 2 contains a differently randomized balanced mixture of Group A and Group B samples">
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span>
      <span class="well group-a">A</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-b">B</span><span class="well group-a">A</span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="plate-legend"><span><i class="swatch group-a"></i> Group A</span><span><i class="swatch group-b"></i> Group B</span></div>
<figcaption id="good-caption"><strong>Better:</strong> every plate supports the comparison, and no group repeatedly occupies one region of the plate.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

The diagrams are intentionally simplified and do not represent an operational
SomaScan plate map. Use the actual list of sample wells and fixed control wells
provided by the laboratory running the assay.

## What to balance

Start with the variables required by the primary analysis. Depending on the
study, these may include:

- primary group, treatment arm, or phenotype;
- collection site or cohort;
- sex, age band, ancestry, or another major biological stratum;
- visit or time point, while keeping repeated samples from the same participant
  linked appropriately for the study objective;
- collection date, freezer location, extraction batch, or other known handling
  factors; and
- technical replicates or bridge samples, when used.

Not every variable can be perfectly balanced. Prioritize the primary contrast,
avoid empty group-by-plate combinations, and involve the statistician and assay
laboratory before the final map is locked.

## Recommended workflow

1. **Define the model first.** State the primary contrast and the covariates or
   blocking variables that the analysis will need.
2. **Obtain the operational plate template.** Mark the wells reserved for assay
   controls and identify the actual study-sample capacity.
3. **Create representative blocks.** Allocate each plate approximately the same
   proportions of the major study groups.
4. **Randomize within constraints.** Randomize study samples over the available
   wells while checking rows, columns, edges, and processing order.
5. **Audit the proposed map.** Cross-tabulate every important variable against
   plate and, where relevant, row and column.
6. **Freeze and export the map.** Save the random seed, script, final plate map,
   deviations from the plan, and the map actually run.
7. **Retain technical variables.** Include plate, well, run, and relevant QC
   outputs in the analysis-ready metadata.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A useful audit question

If one plate failed completely, would the primary biological comparison still
exist in the remaining plates? If the answer is no, revisit the allocation.
:::

## Minimum metadata to retain

Keep, at minimum, a stable sample identifier, participant identifier, study
group, collection site and time, processing timestamps, fasting state,
freeze-thaw count, storage location, shipment, assay run, plate, row, column,
and any departure from the planned workflow. Use explicit missing values rather
than interpreting a blank as “no event.”
